utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom, this is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before I give you an opportunity to cross-examine the witness, Mr. Kehoe, and other Defence counsel and Prosecution, there may have been some confusion about the week of the 16th of June where the Prosecution has on its list no witnesses where, however, the court calendar apparently suggests that we are sitting that week. We are not sitting the week of the 16th to the 20th of June just for your information. Then, Mr. Elleby, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, I want to ask you some questions about some of the matters discussed by the Prosecutor and a little bit about your statements, some of the items in your statements. So if it jumps around a bit there is some methodology to it. I want to talk to you a little bit first about a period of time before Operation Storm in July of 1995 and I understand from your statement you came in the latter part of June 1995?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mid-May, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mid-May, excuse me, mid-May, 1995. So you were there throughout the build up in July of 1995. Now, in the period you were there, the treatment of the Croatian minorities in the area that you were patrolling was pretty poor, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Treatment of the Croatian minorities was one of our big concerns and we tried to monitor especially the rural areas where especially elderly people lived alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And -- well, if we could bring up P-218 that's already in evidence. This is a UNCIVPOL report from the 24 to the 30 of July. Let me just go to the next page, Mr. Registrar, it will give him the dates here. Do you see that date there, sir, and I just want to take you to three pages in which is the cases monitored including human rights violations. If we can flip up two more pages. One more page. If he can just take that top paragraph Sector South there, it notes that in Sector South, the Croat minority situation in the sector is seemingly worse than that of the Serb minority in south-west. Now, Mr. Elleby, had this pattern of abuse of the Croat minorities gone on for some time as you understood the situation in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that, and also there were a lot of restrictions of movements so from time to time, we couldn't move into certain areas and as this paper shows, in the end of July, we couldn't actually move anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just -- we'll touch on the restriction of movements in one moment but I'd just like to talk to you a little bit about the reporting on what was occurring with the Croat minority in the Krajina or in Sector South which is the area that you were familiar with. What exactly was transpiring and what was being reported back and what did you learn?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any cases reported but the Croatian minority had difficulties getting daily needs, food supply, if they needed any medical treatments, there were no infrastructure securing that they could go to, for example, Knin to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So there was some, for instance, inabilities to go to the hospital in Knin if they needed medical care?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And while you were driving around the Sector South area and again I'm talking about before Operation Storm, did you observe widespread destruction of Croat villages and towns?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some houses in some towns destructed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Elleby, taking off on your restriction of movement point, before we get to that, the relationship between CIVPOL and the RSK authorities was pretty poor for a significant period of time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was changing. It was going up and down, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I mean and -- let's focus on July, it was -- and what was happening in July of 1995. It was very poor in July of 1995, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the RSK authorities restricted UNCIVPOL's ability to go where they wanted to go to do their job, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as tensions moved or as tensions grew in the Knin area, the restrictions were virtually eliminated, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In addition to that, there were hijackings of UN vehicles, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, while this was going on, you were also aware, were you not, that the HV, the army of the -- you understand HV is --

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- the HV is a -- it's always good to clarify to make sure we're on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The HV was -- had a series of offensives through July up through the Dinara towards Grahovo that caused the ARSK to be defeated in a series of attacks, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last part of your sentence I don't know, but I knew that the Croatian army was advancing into the Dinara area in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, before we explore that a little bit more let me just talk to you a little bit about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, may I just seek some clarification. One of your questions was and it may be a lack of knowledge of the English language on my part and as tensions moved or as tensions grew in the Knin area, the restrictions were virtually eliminated. Were the restrictions eliminated or was the freedom of movement eliminated?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was a good catch, Judge, I believe we were talking about the freedom of movements were eliminated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Here you see if you apparently use the wrong terms and you get of course then the wrong answer and everyone seems to be fully happy and not being aware of what was said anymore. The Chamber tries to stay aware of the words used. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise, Judge, and I thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now talking about Knin itself, Knin itself, the population in Knin was armed, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think -- yes, maybe some civilian also were armed. I couldn't answer that totally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. But based on your relationship with the population in Knin, the population in Knin throughout July of 1995 was certainly very hostile towards you and other UN members, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorities were quite hostile. The civil population a bit less. I mean we were actually staying in their houses and living between them through the day and it didn't give any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And why were the authorities hostile towards the UN?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it can only be a guess. I guess they didn't like us being there or they wanted to keep something from us. Could have been military movement. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to that in a moment. But just staying with the population in Knin. You were attempting to work with the RSK police during this period of time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And during this period of time, did you observe the RSK police virtually switching uniforms from their normal blue uniforms to switching to green combat fatigues?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that happened at several occasions for shorter or longer periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So would you -- did you conclude from that that they were blending their police functions and their military functions together?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was sometimes difficult to see the difference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you are asking the witness for conclusions in relation to functions and apparently you started with the uniforms they were wearing. Now, these are of course two different things, what uniform you wear or what functions you are performing. Could you please lay a proper foundation and where the witness answered, "It was sometimes difficult to see the difference," then it's unclear whether he is referring to the uniforms or to the performance of functions and I think that's important for us to know. But perhaps, Mr. Elleby, having heard this you could clarify. Was the difficulty to see the performance in functions or was it difficult to see the difference in the uniforms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the last option, Your Honour, it was difficult to see who was who. I wasn't totally aware of the functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as we move through July of 1995, you note in your supplemental information sheet -- well actually, I think it begins in P214, page 1 about midway down, that you saw a lot of soldiers on the street but I'm -- in your supplemental sheet, you note that you observed an increased number of RSK troops in Knin in this period -- in the period building up to the beginning of Operation Storm. Can you tell us about that a little bit?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the assessment of the picture in the streets, in the town, was that from a few days in July and up to the end of July, that there came more and more military vehicles, more and more uniformed military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you and your other CIVPOL monitors observe that while you were driving around the area?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this is, if we go back to 218, and on page 3, if I may. I believe that's the same page, just towards the bottom of -- if we can go to the next page, please. In the quality of life -- I don't know if we could give the witness an ability to see that bottom portion a little bit better. Can you see that, Mr. Elleby? I know that's a little cut off on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The second sentence says, "A similar situation --" well, let me read the prior sentence first because it puts the next sentence into context. "The quality of life in sectors north and south has been dramatically affect by the imminent threat of war. Towns in Sector North look like ghost towns, all stores and public places being closed with only women, children and the aged or handicapped left at homes. A similar situation exists in Sector South where the natives are reported to be nervous and increasingly hostile towards the UN." So this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I take it that you wanted to read that it had drastically instead of dramatically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, drastically. Did I misread that? Yes, drastically, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So this is essentially taking place when you are at least learning about the fighting that's going up on the Dinara; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So at the same time, and correct me if I converge these ideas improperly in any fashion, so while you were learning of fighting up in the Dinara, and an increase of personnel, of soldiers in Knin, the civilian population is becoming increasingly hostile towards the UN. Is that all basically happening at the same time?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say as I look at it and as I remember it that the civil population were hostile to UN, but they were desperate and they were getting more and more nervous. That was obvious. And the authorities maybe were a little more hostile than the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, things -- did things dramatically change after the fall of Bosanski Grahovo on the 27th, 28th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be Sector East?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's actually over in Bosnia but right over the Dinara.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during this period of time when you were observing the increase in troops in Knin, and you might have said this before, Mr. Elleby, but could you give us a bit of a time frame of when you saw this increase in troops?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was beginning in maybe the first or the second week of July and then it was increasing until the last days of July when they were there were quite a lot of military in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, during this period of time, did you notice troop movements up the road from Knin towards Strmica and basically up the road to Strmica?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of troop movements. I couldn't give the purpose for where they were going but they were moving in and out of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Basically a direction, did you see troop movements going out of Knin towards Strmica?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see military equipment going up that road towards Strmica as well?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember very clearly but there were some tanks also in the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During this period of time and if we could back to P118 on this, excuse me, P218.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarifying question? You were talking -- you were asked about civilian population in the part of your report where it is about quality of life. You are talking about natives, natives getting nervous, natives becoming hostile. Did you have all the natives on your mind? Were you thinking about certain ethnicities? Because in the context, reading it, it might well refer to certain natives but that's not what this portion of -- says. Could you tell us whether nervosity and whether hostility was equally on both sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to, Your Honour. First, I will say the document on the screen, I didn't write it, it's an assessment from the HQ in Zagreb gathering up information from all the sectors. Our contact with the civilian population in the period before Operation Storm was basically a Serb population. If there were any Croats staying in Knin, it must have been very few. I don't remember. But all the places the monitors were accommodated were at Serbian families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So as far as you're concerned, your answers were about Serbs and Serbian families?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, staying with this document, the next sentence after the one we just read beginning with "early successes," do you see that, sir? "Early successes" is cut off a just a bit, Mr. Monkhouse, but it notes that, "Early successes in a Croatian attack on either Sector South and Sector North could easily initiate mass hysteria or panic in turn leading to random violence against the UN personnel living there." Now, Mr. Elleby, is that an accurate assessment of what you thought would happen if the HV began to move in towards the Knin area and had some success in a military campaign?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were discussions in the HQ in Knin, the UN HQ whether or not there would be a hostage situation. I don't remember any fear among the UN personnel from the civil population that they would take any hostile action against us but, again, it was very tense. Everybody was very nervous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But what we have in this report is reporting back from the Sector South unit to Zagreb, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as we move through the rest of this paragraph, it says, "The forced closure of businesses not to mention the critical cut off of the Livno valley supply route is bound to have an adverse socio-economic effects. Is bound to have adverse socio-economic effects. The road through Bosanski Grahovo was the main smuggling pipeline to Knin." Now, what was the -- and I take it that this is a smuggling pipeline by the RSK to Knin. Now, do you recall what was being brought down -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall what was being smuggled into Knin through the Bosanski Grahovo road?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could just go down to the last sentence, it notes that, "The influx of refugees from Bosanski Grahovo and Strmica is further destabilizing the civil situation in Knin." Do you recall when these refugees left Bosanski Grahovo and Strmica and began to make their way into Knin?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when these tensions were rising, was there a basic fear of the Croats retaking this area, a fear among the Krajina Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And based on the period of time you were living there, was there a degree of propaganda coming from the Krajina Serb authorities about what would transpire if the Croats ultimately came into the area?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say I only heard of that sort of propaganda. I didn't read the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand it very well. But I think -- that's speculation, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I think I heard was that it would be a very bad for the Serb population when the Croatian army would take back Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, did you conclude at the time, Mr. Elleby, that that increased the tension level among the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could you please make a small pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I apologise, Mr. Elleby, you and I are speaking English but apparently I'm moving a bit too quickly and I'll do what I can to take a pause between our comments to each other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, in this period of time, did you observe the Serb population leaving the area on buses?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if I may, I just would like to cover a couple of areas that you talked about yesterday and the -- well, yesterday, excuse me. And basically, you talked about Operation Storm when it took place. In your testimony -- Your Honour, I only have the preliminary version of the transcript because the final has not come out yet. But on yesterday's transcript at page 51, line 25 going on to page 52, line 1, you noted that, "I remember the UN military talking about a very fast and professional military operation." Do you also recall, sir, that after that took place, there was also a talk about a counterattack by the ARSK and/or the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that issue being discussed at the staff meetings with the UN military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did they talk about the ARSK joining with the Bosnian Serb forces to conduct such a counterattack?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that in detail. They were -- the UN military were trying to assess the possibility of an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. Now, in P225, if we could bring that up on the screen. Mr. Elleby, this is the document that we talked yesterday, your 16 August 1995 report that you signed at the bottom. But you note in the first sentence that, "Ten days have gone since the Croatian invasion in Knin. It is pretty clear that most of the soldiers have been sent out of the town." Now, Mr. Elleby, at this point are you talking about the soldiers that initially came into Knin on the 5th of August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. This should assess that the picture in the streets were changing so there were less military personnel and more and more police and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you learn either through observation or conversations with either personnel on the street or at the UN compound that the soldiers, the HV soldiers had been redeployed to an area up on the border between Croatia and Bosnia to prepare to take defensive positions and prepare against the counterattack?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, staying with this document, this is the document that you note towards the second to last paragraph that you noted that it was like a Tombstone, Arizona, and there was a -- by that, you inferred that there was a degree of lawlessness and chaos in the area, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would you consider it to be a power vacuum during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you call it, but it was discussed in the UN compound that it was still quite unsafe to be in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think you talked about a variety of -- and we'll talk about some lootings and burnings that were going on there but amidst this chaos, and correct me if in any way I make a mistake on commenting on your testimony, but within this chaos, did you observe that there were, in fact, attempts by some Croat authorities to bring some order to what was transpiring in Knin and the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer to that that I think that some of the authorities were working hard on it. It was not clear to me as a UN officer to see the progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. But the -- based on your testimony, there were some authorities that were working hard to bring some order here. But let's turn to a document that was admitted into evidence but was not discussed yesterday which is P224.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, your last line said that, "Based on your testimony, there was some authorities ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That clearly was the testimony of that witness, based on the witness to establish anything is for the Chamber to do. I don't know why you repeated it, perhaps because you think it important. This Chamber finds all the evidence important and not just those portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then "based on the testimony" really suggests that you are qualifying it as something which is true and good and that's, again, for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And already in your previous sentence, you said, "Forgive me on commenting," you were perfectly right that commenting is not needed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was inviting the witness if at any portion I, in my question, inferred something contrary to his testimony, I invited him to correct me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Put that question, he answered that question very clearly and that's it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn to P224. Now, this is a report, a UNCIVPOL report dated 15 August 1995, and the second sentence down, well, actually, "On 13 August 1995, at 11.45, human rights patrol visited Ivosevci area in the hamlet of Korolije," giving a grid reference, "met with four Serb old people who remained in the area. They informed that the Croatian army CA present there, which includes one doctor, has been feeding them and treating them well." In the midst of this chaos, there were reports like that, Mr. Elleby, where the Croatian army was attempting to assist the Serb population, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this report shows it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you learn of other reports in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You talked a little bit in your statements and a bit in your testimony about some lootings and burnings transpiring and if I could bring up a series of reports and if we could start with, if I may, I think I missed a P number for 65 ter 2105. I have been told that it's still a 65 ter document and has not been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you would like to tender that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D237.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D237 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, on the -- if we could pull this document up. I don't believe this is the document I am referring to and I may have been mistaken on this document. It is a Sector South weekly report from -- I am mistaken, Judge, if we can strike D237, it has been admitted into evidence as P223. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please vacate D237.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the report. If we can go in, just the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As you can see, Mr. Elleby, this is a weekly report of 14-20 of August 1995. And if we could go in two more pages to the 15th of August. That's it. And I know that there is a copying line through there, Mr. Elleby, which might render it a bit difficult to see, but nevertheless, frankly that's the best we have. If you could look at that comment under "unfortunately ..."

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you see that, "Unfortunately, the trend of robbery and intimidation of remaining Serbs has been initiated in Sector South. A Serb living in Knin AOR was assaulted and robbed at his house by a group of four Croats, two of whom were soldiers." Now, looking at this particular item, it has an incident that takes place with four Croats. I infer from that that two were in civilian clothing and two of them were in military clothing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, I don't remember the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was it very common when you heard reports of civilian people in civilian clothing operating or doing something criminal with people that were wearing combat fatigues?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, in this particular incident, when you -- did you -- obviously when you read this at the time, you would have -- would you have concluded that this was not some military operation if we had people in civilian clothing and military clothing operating together?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you are reading -- you are drawing an inference and you are asking the witness to follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The report says that they were soldiers. Of course it's likely that you call soldiers those who are wearing uniforms, but you make an inference and want the witness to follow that. I'd like to know do you have any knowledge of why these two persons were qualified in this report as soldiers? Do you know whether it was on the basis of the uniform? Do you know whether it was on the basis of knowledge of the reporter that they were soldiers? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Inferences are there to be drawn by the Chamber on an accurate, factual basis. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you note in -- actually, it is -- in P225, if we may go back to that. You note at P225, sir, that you observed a soldier taking a stereo. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in that, sir, when you saw that particular item, you saw somebody that was in fatigues; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you translate fatigues for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In military clothing?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And based on seeing this person taking this stereo, you didn't conclude that he was conducting some type of military operation, did you?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, likewise, if we go to 227, P227, in this particular instance, in the second paragraph down, it notes, and this is from the 17th of August, 1995, "Consequently, there is material evidence that the houses in question were set ablaze by Croatian infantrymen as six of them were seen on board a tractor and driving from the scene towards the main road." Were you familiar with this incident, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As a -- one of the supervisors for UN CIVPOL at the time, if you had read an item such as this, six men identified as Croatian infantry seen on board of a tractor, would you have concluded that they were doing this on their own?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would be speculation. I don't remember my reaction to this report which I obviously must have read at the time. I don't know the culture, the behaviour of soldiers on the Balkans. I don't know if they could do such a thing. So I would have trouble answering that in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me take you to a UNCRO report, actually it's an UNMO report, P154. Now, this is a situation report, Mr. Elleby, from the 19th of September, 1995, and I'm not saying that you saw this report, Mr. Elleby, there is just some information in here that I'd like to ask you about. If we could go three pages in. And up at the point E, the next page, please. In the humanitarian aspects, 19 at 820 September, investigated one house on fire in Knin," grid reference. "No casualties observed. It is assessed that the house was set on fire by neighbours returning to the area. Now, Mr. Elleby, was that a general impression of the CIVPOL authorities, including yourself, that much of or at least some of these fires were -- or took place and were done by neighbours, Croat neighbours who were returning to the area after having been exiled some years before?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I can only say that there were a lot of houses burning in the area in that period. I didn't, myself, see anyone put fire to any one of those houses. I didn't witness it. And this is an UNMO assessment. I don't know on what base it is made on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I just take it one step further, Mr. Elleby. When you had discussions between and among your colleagues and CIVPOL and UNMO, did such an impression come into the conversation that many of the crimes that were taking place in Sector South were being done by Croats returning to the area?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just going down a little bit more to the UNMO Sibenik team. It notes, "When distributing food to remaining Serbs in the following villages," and gives the villages, "observed men in civilian and uniforms looting the villages." Was that also a -- was that an assessment of your personnel when you were in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That the civilians and soldiers or people in uniform, if you will, were doing this together?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me go to the next page of this document. It is right in the centre of that page and it's the same situation report, Mr. Elleby, on the 19th of September. Just starting from, "But the remaining Serbs can observe lootings of neighbours' houses." Do you see that, sir? In the middle of -- just a little bit down. "The remaining Serbs can observe looting of ..."

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "But the remaining Serbs can observe looting of neighbours' houses. The remaining Serbs states that the area earlier have been visited by HV soldier that behaved in a correct manner, but they believed that the uniformed men visiting now are not real soldiers." That particular instance of people in uniform that you, CIVPOL, which either on patrol or part of HRAT patrols, was that a conclusion that simply because these people were in uniform they weren't necessarily real soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be difficult for me or any other CIVPOL officer to tell the difference unless somebody was wearing jeans and sneakers and just a military coat or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So can I take from your answer that simply because somebody had what looked to be like a military uniform, you couldn't conclude that that person was actually a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, were you familiar with Kari Anttila who was not only an UNMO but was, I guess, working on the HRAT patrols? He was a Finnish gentleman there during the same time frame as you, possibly coming in mid-August?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He testified, I believe, on the 2nd of May before this Court on page 2646 and starting on line 13, that was referring to a comment in his witness statement that, "Croats were burning and looting Serb houses independent on their military activity." The question is, "You meant independent of their military activity?" And he answered, "Yes." "So these Serbs" actually, the Croat but, "these soldiers were doing it completely independent of what their responsibilities were militarily, weren't they?" Answer: "That's what I've tried to say there." So, sir, when you were down in Sector South in your position, did you likewise conclude as Mr. Anttila that this looting and burning of Serb houses by people in uniform was done completely independent of military responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't be able to conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, but the incident that you had talked to us about is the Puma Brigade situation or the looting of your -- or the stealing of your landlady's car. You have to --

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you were, I believe, shown an exhibit which is P281. Now, you noted in response to Judge Orie's question that you could only identify the actual animal that's in this; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you were shown this picture by the Office of the Prosecutor, were you shown any other photographs?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you were asked about this incident, and you observed your landlady's car being stolen, and you saw -- and it was people that were -- looked like military uniforms? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you conclude at that point when you observed that these people in uniforms were stealing this car on their own and not as part of some military function?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think they were stealing that car on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us talk a little bit about some of the reports that you filed and you talked about yesterday. And I address your attention to P179.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you are asking the witness for a conclusion. He said what he thought. Could we try to lay a factual foundation for that? Could you tell us how many there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As I remember, there were four soldiers, young men in uniform with the Puma on the shoulder. Some of them were wearing soft military caps. At least one of them has a scarf tied around his head instead of a hat or a cap on it. And they were -- all four were armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they in company with people who were not in military attire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see persons in similar uniforms in the vicinity, I mean not directly together with these four, but -- well, let's say, in the next street or in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't recognise exactly these four soldiers with other soldiers, but soldiers dressed like the four were seen in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If soldiers were present in the area, did you observe soldiers patrolling in groups of a similar size?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any patrolling, didn't look like patrolling, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why did it not look like patrolling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More looked like, so to say, that the soldiers were hanging around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Elleby, this incident that you told us about, about this theft of your landlady's car, this was a single incident of theft, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let's us turn our attention to some of the documents that we talked about with the Prosecutor and I want to focus on a couple of reports that you put into evidence and if I could look at P179.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Take that off, please. Take it down, please. Excuse me, P235. I'm sorry. D179, D.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, a couple of questions about this, Mr. Elleby. I think you talked about this document previously as a list of murders that were committed since the 4th that you sent on to Mr. Cetina in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think that you also said in response to my learned friend's comments that you weren't clear as to what happened with this information after you sent it.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this information is based on information UN CIVPOL gathered at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And certainly, it wasn't making any conclusions about whether or not these were, in fact, murders or that the information you were passing along was accurate; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information passed along was accurate as it was taken from the inc-reps, whether or not all of them were murder cases should be shown through the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. Let's -- if we could go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In 179 on -- this is three pages in on 13. Is this D179, I'm sorry? Excuse me, P179. 13 on the bottom, this again is the listing of the items that you sent on to Mr. Cetina. In this particular item, you are talking about an incident that took place on the 21st of August where an individual was found in a well. Do you recall this, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall this being reported to me, this incident, about the person in the well, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And again, it's incident report 02-95/477. Now, if we could turn to that particular document which is P233. Now, if you take a quick look at this, sir, this is a document that refers to an individual -- two men dressed in civilian clothing coming into the village with long hair and carrying AK-47s. And as we move down the line towards the second to last paragraph, it talks about these CIVPOL officers going to the village and there was a victim inside the well. Do you see that towards the bottom, "Today, on 23 August, 1995"?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "At 1000 hours, CIVPOL went to Benkovac and was accompanied by military police from CanBat and Policija Benkovac to the scene of the crime. The victim was still inside the well. She was brought out of the well and on close examination, there was no visible sign of gunshot wounds." Now, if we move up just a bit in that paragraph, apparently this woman had left her cane and her apron neatly folded and her shoes were placed on top. Now, when you say that this was a list of murders, I mean the list that you sent to Mr. Cetina was a list of murders, did you question in your mind whether or not this fit the category of a murder or of a woman who just committed suicide?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, as long as no thorough investigation has been taken place, you couldn't be sure that it is murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Right. And would that likewise be in P229, if you could put P229. This describes a woman that when approached by two HV soldiers ran and was shot. While it's described as a murder, all you're asking for in this report is further investigation with no conclusion that this was, in fact, a murder; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the witness has now on three occasions told us that he reported those incidents where apparently, persons were killed and where, on the basis of the reporting, it appeared to be justified to further investigate because the possibility of a murder could certainly not be excluded. That's apparent from all these stories. Why go through all that? I mean that's what he said what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I will move on to my last topic because I'm almost done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we go to P223. Now, Mr. Elleby, you did, in fact, learn that arrests of some HV soldiers had been made during this time frame, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just -- if we can go to the next page in this document. I want to make sure the date is correct. It's -- can we change that to P230. If we can go -- if I can just check this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour. If we go to the next page of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we can -- this is another -- a weekly report coming from Zagreb and if we can go three more pages in. If we can just -- if you see the "Yet" there, sir and if we go down to that sentence, the next sentence says, "Knin Policija." Do you see that about three quarters of the way down, further down. It's about the middle -- do you see "Knin Policija liaison officer Gambiroza Zvonko"?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Has however mentioned to UNCIVPOL a case of three HV soldiers being arrested for theft and arson in Korenica." So obviously that report was coming out of Korenica but it was in fact happening that soldiers were arrested?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this before but -- and I don't remember but, yes, it looked like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, we talked a bit about during the course of your testimony with my learned friend Mr. Kay about a series of reports going on within the civilian authorities and you expressed your frustration in trying to get things done because you weren't learning what was transpiring in these investigations, were you?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think you noted that in some of the areas, the higher echelon areas of the Croatian civilian police would have or should have been contacted by the people at the UN in Zagreb and not you on a low level; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And based on your experience, I mean you had some difficult times dealing with the UN bureaucracy in Zagreb, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were some bureaucracy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you had a difficult time getting information from them as well?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I think we had a good connection with the commissioner's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The information that was -- you certainly -- I think you said yesterday in response to Mr. Kay you weren't getting information back on these investigations and if we could look at D97. And I -- I know you haven't seen this report, sir, but I just have you take a look at D97, it's a report from Minister Jarnjak of the Ministry of the Interior to the state Prosecutor and if you take a look at the first page and then take a look at the second page. The second page the two boxes: One, overview of crimes punishable acts according to the police administration, 22 August to 2 October 1995. And the next box is the statistics on overview of number of on-site investigations and perpetrator profile for the same time frame. Now, recognising that you hadn't seen this document, Mr. Elleby, would it be fair to say that you would have been much more satisfied that work was being done on these investigations had you been made aware of these statistics and this information?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you weren't made aware of it?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I appreciate your time. You have been very helpful. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you assist me, known perpetrators appear in three categories. Could you give us a clue as what you understand known perpetrators in their three different categories to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will have Mr. Misetic look at the B/C/S and it has a designation there in B/C/S and he can read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It appears not on the translation, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, under known perpetrators it says -- the first column says, "Members of the HV." The second column says, "Civilians." And the third column says, "Misuse of uniform," in other words, it would indicate a person who was improperly wearing a uniform at the time of commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I have to understand this that only in one case in this period of time, for example, in Zadar-Knin that it was established that someone who was wearing a uniform abused that uniform so that all others wearing uniforms were not abusing that uniform and therefore were soldiers? Is that how I have to understand this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Quite frankly, Your Honour, I'm not certain of that. It may just be that someone had presented themselves -- misrepresented themselves officially upon being asked to state who they are, that they represented themselves as a member of the HV and then also were charged with making a false representation, sort of like impersonating a police officer as opposed to simply wearing a camouflage shirt or pants and then being categorised as a civilian. I would have to look into that further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm asking this because of course you are presenting these statistics to the witness and I take it that you want to tender that, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's actually in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this of course is for a time frame of 22 August to 2 October and not prior to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. Because if the statistics are there, we now know that this witness was not aware of these statistics but these statistics are now in evidence so we try to interpret them and we try to understand them. Thank you, Mr. Kehoe, for -- Ms. Frolich. Is there any need to reexamine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Elleby, Ms. Frolich will put some further questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Elleby, yesterday you said that you believe that Mr. Romanic was key for you to get a move on in the policing of crimes and that was in response to a question page 38, lines 7 and 8, in response to a question from Mr. Kay, you said that you appreciated that the dead bodies that you found and asked to be investigated would have to be investigated not by his Kotar-Knin police administration but by the Zadar-Knin police administration. Your answer was, "I did, of course, but I still found that he was the key for us to get a move on in the policing of these matters." Now, can you tell us why you still considered Mr. Romanic to be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry, maybe I'm too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, did you hear my question or should I repeat part of it?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I understand your question. I -- my opinion was that Mr. Romanic was my point of contact, so to say, in the area of Knin. In a bureaucracy system, it's quite normal that you make contacts on your own level and then the person you contact will move on in his system. And being a police officer, I didn't think that Mr. Romanic would neglect information about dead people.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What exactly did you expect Mr. Romanic to do about the information that you gave him?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expected him to pass the information on to the investigation department, wherever it was, and to get information back what was happening in the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Would this information be any information on what was happening in the case?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wish was that we could discuss progresses in the policing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What was the role of Mr. Cetina in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was above Mr. Romanic and if Mr. Romanic couldn't tell us about the progressing in the policing, we had to ask Mr. Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: How do you expect Mr. Cetina to know about information that you provided to Mr. Romanic?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expected that Mr. Romanic and Mr. Cetina shared information regularly, daily or anyway, often, because Mr. Cetina was above Mr. Romanic for the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And how did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know it. I just -- I just hoped that it and I hoped that we could get a move on in the information to and fro the CIVPOL so we knew what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: But something gave you the impression that Mr. Cetina was above Mr. Romanic. What was that?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't actually remember how I got to that knowledge. I think Mr. Romanic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's a matter that's within the witness's statement presented in 92 ter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, it appears that Mr. Kay considers it not necessary to ask questions same as what is in already evidence in the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I will try not to waste the Court's time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Elleby, you were asked questions yesterday about the reporting procedure to the civilian police. On page 63, especially lines 24 and 25. Now, I would like to show you two documents and could we please pull up P253. And I note that the original of this document is in B/C/S. If we could zoom out a little bit. Mr. Elleby, do you recognise this document? Could we go to page 2 in both English and B/C/S. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the document. I remember -- sorry, I recognise the sign of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, who is the signator of this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the commander of the UNCIVPOL Knin station, Mr. Petro Romasev.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to the first page. Who is this document addressed to?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's addressed to Mr. Mihic in the Knin police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Elleby, what does this document seem to represent?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to represent a reporting of findings that Mr. Romasev has been doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, based on what you said yesterday about the reporting procedure to the civilian police, you said you did not remember clearly what the procedure was in all cases. But is this a report that -- is this a kind of a report that would have been received -- the kind of notice that would have been received from CIVPOL, by the CIVPOL -- by the Knin police station from CIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, on a matter here, could that be elaborated, the kind of information. The date of the correspondence is the 8th of September, the first matter raised is the 7th of August and I -- in my respectful submission, it needs elaboration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I expect it, as a matter of fact. Ms. Frolich, you would ask whether this document refreshes the memory of the witness in relation to reporting. Could you please lay a proper factual foundation for any conclusions to be drawn from this document as being a kind of document typical for reporting?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, what do you see at the top of the page of this document? Could we go up a little bit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, Ms. Frolich, if there is something in the document, the Chamber can read. The witness can read. You can read. The Defence counsel can read. Then just read and say on the top, it reads so and so and so and then put your question to the witness. Because also the other question to whom it was addressed. It's addressed to the commander of the Knin police station. That's clear, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, is this a UNCIVPOL document? You see that it says UNCIVPOL Sector South Knin station. Does this look like a CIVPOL document to you?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a document made afterwards because the lack of functioning computers, that's why you don't see the letterhead. I think it is based on notes made on the dates mentioned but I find it genuine. I mean the sign of it. I recognise Mr. Petro Romasev's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, what kind of notice do you recall would CIVPOL staff give to civilian police?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refreshes my memory a bit but I still don't remember clearly if this was what we were doing but, of course, the task was to pass on the information of the findings made in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Was this information in written or in oral form?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was both.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could we go to P262. I have the same question about this document. What is this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's similar to the other one. It has another date on it and some other incidents. I can't see the bottom of it, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Could we go to the bottom and -- to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not actually signed but -- okay, on the translated --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If you could look at the original version which is in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the sign of Mr. Romasev, signature, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Again, if you could refresh the Chamber's memory. Who were the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber's memory is perfectly all right, Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Who were the CIVPOL -- on what CIVPOL levels would CIVPOL staff impart information to the civilian police? Which members of CIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The station commander, which here is Mr. Petro Romasev would give the information to the Knin police station commander in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Elleby. Is this document a CIVPOL document from your -- from what you see on the face of this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a genuine document made by Mr. Petro Romasev.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is -- should we take a break at this point or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on how much more time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Probably about 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 10 to 15 minutes. Then we'll have a break until 11.00 and always try to keep everyone to the lower estimate, Ms. Frolich, although I must admit that I failed with Mr. Kehoe this morning. So please try to finish then in ten minutes and again, what everyone can read can just be put to the witness and then questions asked to him. We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, before I allow you to proceed, I'd like to tell you that if you feel that my comments are confusing you or disturbing you, you may refresh my memory as to how it felt to be in this very same courtroom dealing with your first witnesses. I still remember how that felt. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, yesterday, when asked by Mr. Kuzmanovic about the incident in the village of Grubori, which was -- the document shown to you was P230 and on page 100, lines 4 to 8, you said, "I cannot explain why Mr. Romasev wrote this about that it should be committed by Croatian special forces." Question: "It seems to be at least as of the date of this document somewhat of a rush to judgement, don't you think?" Your answer was "Yes." When did you first hear about this incident, Mr. Elleby?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember hearing about the incident in the mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Were you involved in any way in reporting on this incident or investigation of this incident?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. This is one of many cases happening in the period which have passed my desk but I don't recall this in specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And how do you know that Mr. Romasev's conclusion was a rushed one or a rush to judgement?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Romasev do not explain in the writing why he is making that conclusion but he might have had his reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you were asked by Mr. Kuzmanovic about restriction of movement that was imposed in times in CIVPOL, starting, I believe, on page 84 of the original numbering. How did CIVPOL restriction of movement imposed on CIVPOL compare to restriction of movement imposed, for example, on other UN agencies, organisations in the sector?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression is that the restrictions of movement was concerning everybody but from time to time it was different between, for example, between CIVPOL and the UNMOs which were military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes we discussed the necessity of visiting certain areas and as far as I remember, sometimes the UNMOs couldn't go there and then the CIVPOL went instead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, in your statements P215 and P217, you talk about fires in the area that you had under your mandate and yesterday, you told us that you discussed fires with your monitors. Where did your monitors observe these fires?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They observed the fires in the whole area because in the beginning, when they were only allowed to move in Knin and then as the days went on, further and further out, then they observed the fires there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: You mentioned -- you were asked by Mr. Kuzmanovic on page 90, line 16, the question was, "Your teams were restricted by the special police from -- you say that your teams were restricted by the special police from entering certain areas. Where were your teams restricted and on what dates?" Now, why did the monitors go to these areas which were restricted or attempt to go to these areas?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went to the areas because we tried to -- as we were allowed to move out into the sector to cover every area, especially areas we knew there were living people, mainly elderly people, and that was the reason to go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Was there any special reason other special reason other than -- any specific reason to go to the areas that they did not know specifically what they could find there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, the witness already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I will rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: What if anything could CIVPOL monitors observe from these areas?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task to go into the areas was -- the first priority was the humanitarian priority to see if everybody was well in the remote areas and of course to see if any crime had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Was there anything that could be observed from a distance from these areas?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If I may, show the witness his supplemental information sheet that he provided to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 19th of May, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd like to do that in order to refresh his memory?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, did he say his memory needed to be refreshed? What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Well, I will come to that once --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that about observing from a distance?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If this could be placed on the ELMO, please, because I don't believe it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, refreshing his memory is giving it to him and asking him if it refreshes his recollection. He can look at the hard copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see. I do agree with you, Mr. Kehoe, that Ms. Frolich asked me whether she was allowed to show the witness the supplemental information sheet and then I asked whether that was, and my phrasing was not fully correct, whether that was for purposes of seeing whether that statement would refresh the recollection of the witness and that, I think, there's nothing wrong with that. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Now, if you could move the document up a little bit so we could see the bottom half of the document. A little more. That's enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, I would like to turn your attention to the second paragraph from the bottom that is visible on the screen or -- yes, you see it on the screen. The last sentence, "Mr. Elleby also stated that CIVPOL teams were from time to time kept from certain areas where smoke was observed which likely kept them from reporting these incidents of burning." Does that refresh your memory with respect to my question on what could be observed from a distance?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Judge, that's a completely different question than what was asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is not exactly the same but it is in such a way related that the witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think I can clarify it. My first answer was concerning how people was doing in the areas and if crime had happened. That's what I was referring to. It is correct that the monitors from a certain distance could see smoke columns in the area that we were restricted from going into.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you recall when, at what period of time? In what period of time this happened?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in details. In the same period from mid-August to mid-September.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just one more question for you. When you spoke to Mr. Cetina and he gave you his response after you had given him the list of human rights violations and murders, was Mr. Cetina cooperative and responsive to you, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't say that he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Elleby. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Frolich. Have the questions of re-examination triggered any need for further questions by Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No issues arise from the re-examination on my behalf, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Gwaunza first has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, in one of your reports, you noted that you received reports to the effect that it was common to find bodies dumped in wells. Could you just elaborate on that evidence?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It depends on how you're defining "common" at this time. It was seen at some occasions that bodies were dumped in wells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Were there any indications as to statistics relating to such bodies?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that we made any statistics about the status of the findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Kinis has one or more questions for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, I have several questions to you and the first is turning back to your statement, P217, I understand it's February 2008, in paragraph 5, you mentioned about mandate of CIVPOL and there is such wordings I will quote, "... was to supervise civil police work." Could you please clarify what do you mean under term "supervise," was it similar to monitor or do you have more extension of functions?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I -- as I remembered now, supervise is maybe too big a word. It was to monitor or maybe should I say to establish a cooperation with the Croatian police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. And the next issue is in the previous statements, you also mentioned that Croatian side did not provide you information regarding structuring -- structure of police, regarding criminal records, regarding situation on ongoing investigations. Did, at that time, you have some written documents, written agreement between Croatian government and UN which obliged to Croatian side to do it?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was and is still a bit unclear to me. I think I mentioned that the mandate was discussed even in the HQ in Zagreb and I don't remember it being fully clear in the period I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: The last question is: You mentioned that -- also that it was very hard to get some information regarding structure of Croatian police and -- et cetera. My question is do you have -- had, at that time, some training or some knowledge of Croatian legislation, namely, legislation which relates with the development of police or law of police or criminal procedure law which allows to you in legal way to understand functions of these institutions and how you should cooperate with them?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't receive training in that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you as well, Mr. Elleby. The first one is about restrictions of movement. In your testimony yesterday, you explained to us in relation to a report, a weekly report, 21st to 26th of August, and that there was an almost a total freedom of movement starting at that moment approximately, you talked about two to three weeks after Operation Storm. Now, in one of your last answers today, you said when you were explaining what you observed from a distance when no access was -- what at least not what you observed but what was observed from a distance, when you are not given access to a certain area. I think you mentioned -- I'm trying to find it. But you said it was -- do you recall when, at what period of time this happened? And then you gave mid-August to mid-September. And I have some problems in reconciling not getting access to an area where, from a distance, you see smoke and your answers you gave yesterday about the almost total freedom of movement on from the second or third week after Operation Storm. Could you clarify, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to, Your Honour. It is correct that almost freedom of movement was given at the end of August for the CIVPOL to move in and out of the sector and to move around in the sector but as I remember it, from time to time in that same period, certain areas could, in certain periods, be restricted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
