utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I have another question and I'm trying to find the source in yesterday's transcript. Yesterday, questions were asked to you about the Serb resistance. You may remember that I asked you whether it was in hills, woods, or mountains, or whether at all you saw Serb resistance. Now, a short while later a question was put to you about awareness of nine ARSK soldiers were found and also questions were put to you in relation to clean-up or mop-up operations, if I just can find that on page 95 of yesterday's transcript. You were asked what your understanding was and you said: "I understood it that it could be RSK troops in the area." Now, RSK troops, the presence of RSK troops and the presence of RSK soldiers, is that the same as Serbian resistance for you, or is that a different category?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it -- I think that it's -- that is what I meant with it. Well, that's speculation, but of course if there still were Serb soldiers in the area, it would be a resistance to the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So when you use the term "resistance," you would include in resistance ARSK troops that had left that -- had stayed in that area. Now, you told us that you were not aware of whether in mountains, woods, or anywhere else, that you were not aware of the presence of Serb resistance in the area which, as I now understand, includes the presence of ARSK soldiers that had remained there or ARSK troops, perhaps I should say. You explained to us what you understood by a clean-up or a mop-up operation and then a question was put to you, and I will read it literally: "So your understanding of what a clean-up or mop-up operation is is that there were RSK soldiers in the area and beyond that, you have no idea of what the elements of that mop-up operation would be?" You said, "That's right." Now, let me try to analyse with you that question. You were asked about your understanding of what a clean-up or mop-up operation is. That was the first part of that question. And then it follows, it continues in a rather factual way saying: "... is that there were RSK soldiers in the area." Now, what I'd like to clarify with you is the following. Were you saying that you understood a clean-up or a mop-up operation to be an operation in which one would look for the presence of RSK soldiers in the area or was it your understanding that the clean-up and mop-up operations were directed to RSK soldiers of which you were aware that they were present in the area?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of any presence of RSK soldiers and my impression was that the Croatian authority, the military were looking for resistance in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I have no further questions for you. Have the questions by the Bench triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, I'd like to -- part of the questions I have had to put today is because questions were -- the questions I was seeking clarification is because it's not sufficiently exceptional that facts are mixed up sometimes with conclusions or opinions and that the questions are not clear enough in order to get the best answers. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Elleby, you noted in response to a question by Judge Orie that from mid-August to September there were occasional restrictions of movement in the area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were those restrictions of movement to the north as you move up from Knin to Strmica and into -- moving in the direction of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JAN ELLEBY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I remember it, yes, it was the area north of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it was the area north. I'll just take it from there. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Where you confirmed that it was to the north, I understand that to be that it was not to the south, although that is not yet part of that answer. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember those areas being in the north of Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, with the exclusion of the areas south of Knin. Yes, that's how I understood it. That has now been confirmed. Any further questions? Then Mr. Elleby, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for answering a long series of questions by the parties and by the Bench and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd first like to go through the -- meanwhile consolidated list of P exhibits. I have on my list at this moment, and I'll deal with it in terms of P numbers. First series is P218 to and including P224 which are not yet admitted. If there are no specific objections, P218 up to and including P224 are admitted into evidence. P225 is already admitted into evidence. P226 and P227, I've not heard of any specific objections and are therefore admitted into evidence. A decision has already been made on P228, therefore, I continue with P229 to and including P280. No further specific objections which means that P229 to and including P280 are admitted into evidence. A decision has been made already in relation to P281, that was admitted. P282 still to be decided. No specific objections, then P282 is admitted into evidence. P283 and P284 were admitted into evidence already. I think that is a complete list of the documents tendered by the Prosecution. I do not know whether the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just with regard to the -- obviously the -- that were added to the list, of course we are reserving our objection. I guess it was P253 and 262 that they were documents that he didn't know anything about so it was just the same objection we had before. I understand Your Honour has put in that notwithstanding that but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll have to look at them again to see whether there were any other reasons and apparently if a witness doesn't know anything about it, often it comes down to sometimes the witness recognising a type of a document and sometimes, that's at least the way I experience it, it sometimes comes down to a document, an exhibit which attempted is introduced through a witness and if the witness doesn't know anything about, still it has some relevance and probative value as a contemporaneous document and slips in more or less as a document tendered from the bar table. That's what actually happens often. If there is any specific -- apart from that the witness didn't know anything about the documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then we leave it as it is for the time being. Then we received not yet and I'm not urging to do it at this very moment, not -- a response by the Prosecution on the bundle of documents tendered by Mr. Kay, tendered from the bar table. I think you said that you had no objections. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might more be that the Chamber itself will still need some time to check exactly because some translations were still missing and even if the parties agree on relevance and probative value, the Chamber usually has a look at it as well before it decides. Is there any other procedural matter at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's just on that last collection of documents, Your Honour, which we would urge a quick resolution to. The reason being, it ties in with the evidence of the witness and we believe will make it easier to manage affairs as one progresses through the information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- in this trial. If it's possible for the Court to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll try to give it priority. At the same time, the Chamber needs to take some time now and then in order not to follow the parties not considering itself what the Chamber is doing and therefore I ask for a bit more time but we'll give it priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is granted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kay. Generosity is a good thing, isn't it? I should think about that. Anything else at this moment? For the next witness to be called -- yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just wasn't sure when you were talking about procedural matters, Your Honour, there is a motion pending with respect to the next witness, I believe, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a notification for the next witness if I'm well aware but I do not know whether there's any motion pending for the next witness. I know that there is a notification and I was just about to come to that, that the next witness has been granted protective measures in another case, that was face distortion, voice distortion, and pseudonym. And that the Prosecution has notified us of the existence of those protective measures and in accordance with the Rules, they will remain effective in other cases as well unless rescinded, varied or augmented and the notification included that the witness certainly did not give any reasons to rescind or vary it and would rather prefer that they stay as they are which is an automatism under the Rules. That's the situation as far as I understand it. If that's what you were referring to, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I wasn't sure what exact protective measures then applied in this case and also there may have been another reason, if we were going to discuss it, another reason for the protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Rule is, but always have them with me, that if protective measures are granted in one case, they automatically, but if you could -- I'm just -- I was doing it from my -- let me just see. This is Rule ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it's 75.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 75(F), "Once protective measures have been ordered in respect of a victim or witness in any proceedings before the Tribunal, such protective measures shall continue to have effect mutatis mutandis in any other proceedings before the Tribunal or another jurisdiction unless and until they are rescinded, varied or augmented." I think this triple that was still clearly on my mind, rescinded, varied or augmented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just for the record and I don't want to be hyper-technical, I understood that to mean that the witness's testimony in the case in which protective measures were granted would remain covered by protective measures. I note for the record we do not object to the protective measures but just as a procedural matter, and in terms of the right to be heard or the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not a continuation of protective measures, let's say under Rule 92, I always forgot which is the paragraph that deals with relying upon transcripts of earlier testimony. No, it is the protection of the witness himself. That's at least how I understand this Rule. If there's any dispute about this then I'd like to hear from the parties not only that they disagree but also on the basis of what authority they disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There is no disagreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we need sometime to have the protective measures prepared. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could go into private session in relation to a scheduling issue, in relation to the witness after next?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We'll then have a break in which the set-up for the protective measures will be tested and we'll then have one more session to go until a quarter to 2.00. We resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness 56.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From your answer, I understand you can hear me in a language you understand. Witness 56, we'll not call you by your own name. Protective measures have been granted in respect of you that means we will call you Witness 56. We'll avoid whatever identifying information during your public testimony and further, your face cannot be seen outside of this courtroom and your voice is distorted as well. Witness 56, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher now hands out to you the text. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness 56. Please be seated. Will it be you, Ms. Gustafson, who examines the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Ms. Gustafson who is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can we start by showing the witness the pseudonym sheet which is 65 ter number 5166.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under seal not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Witness 56, is that your correct name and birth date on that sheet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I begin my testimony, might I be allowed to state, to express my sympathies with General Gotovina over his father's death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have not dealt with this matter in open court. I appreciate what you just have said. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Witness 56, do you recognise your correct name and birth date on that sheet in front of you on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could that be given an exhibit number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P285, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P285 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown 65 ter number 4862 and if he could be provided with a hard copy of his four statements in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson, I take it also not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Witness 56, do you recognise the statement you see on the screen and the first one you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Is that a statement that you made and signed on the 3rd of December, 1996?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And could the witness be shown 65 ter number 4863, again not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the statement on the screen now as the one you made and signed on the 18th of September, 2000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise that and do acknowledge it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And could the witness now be shown 65 ter number 4864, again not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this statement as one that you made and signed on the 12th of June, 2007?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And finally, if the witness could be shown 65 ter number 5167, again not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this as a statement you made on the 21st of May, 2008?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do these four statements accurately reflect what you said at the time that they were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And taken together, do these -- are these four statements true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if I asked you today in court the same questions you were asked when you gave those statements, would you give the Court the same answers that are in those statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender those four statements into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, the Chamber was informed that the 2000 statement would be redacted, that some portions would be taken out. Is that -- or would you like to tender the full statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct and the one that the witness was shown and the one that's under 65 ter 4863 is redacted pursuant to that agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you only show me the cover page and since we have those -- we have not got those numbers, the Chamber cannot observe that, but I do understand then that -- I think it's from page 2, the second half of page 2 of the statement that there, that's the portion of the content that is -- that you are seeking to tender. Then I take it that the Chamber has to understand the 2008 statement in such a way that to the extent that it corrects what was earlier said, that to that extent, the earlier statement is not accurate, it may reflect what the witness said but is not to the best of his recollection what is the truth and therefore, we focus on that last statement, if it comes to corrections of earlier statements. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just wish to be clear. Your Honour, you said you believe it starts from the second half of page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Seven, I think I may have misspoken, I had 7 on my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I heard two as well. So, it is page 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So most likely I had misspoken. So any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Registrar, numbers for the statements. Let's start with the start with the first one mentioned by Ms. Gustafson, the 1996 statement would be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's 65 ter 04862 and this becomes Exhibit P286.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P286 is admitted into evidence. The next one is the redacted August and September 2000 statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 04863 becomes Exhibit P287, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P287 is admitted into evidence. The third one, the statement of June 2007.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 04864 and that becomes Exhibit P288, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P288 is admitted into evidence. And then finally, the 2008 statement, the supplemental statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's 65 ter 05167 and that becomes Exhibit P289.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P289 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to start with reading a brief summary of the witness's Rule 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll explain to the witness what the purpose of this is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Prior to Operation Storm, aside from elderly males and a few men working in essential civilian posts, the population of Knin was predominantly made up of women and children. Most military-aged males were at the front line. Witness 56 described the 3rd of August, 1995, as a normal day in Knin. On the 4th of August, 1995, Witness 56 was woken by the sound of explosions at 5.00 a.m. After approximately half an hour, he made his

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: shelled. During the day, Witness 56 observed shells falling in Knin as well as shelling damage. During the night of 4th August, 1995, and the early hours of 5th August, Witness 56 travelled from Knin to Benkovac and back towards Knin. In Benkovac, he saw several houses on fire and columns of people moving in the direction of Kistanje. On the way back to Knin, he stopped at the villages of Kistanje and Djevrske which were virtually empty. Witness 56 was told by people there that those villages had been shelled. Witness 56 was not able to reenter Knin in the early morning of 5th August because the road was blocked by vehicles going in the opposite direction. He was forced to follow the convoy leading towards Otric. He eventually reached Bosanski Petrovac at approximately 1900 hours on the 5th of August of, 1995. On about 7th or 8th August, 1995, while he was in Bosanski Petrovac, Witness 56 saw evidence of the convoy being bombed as it was moving towards Bravsko. That concludes the summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first give the interpreters and transcribers one second to breathe and to -- Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could just move into private session for a minute, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: During the private session, the Court has instructed the registry to remove from the public record what was said about the professional activity of this witness. The public in this courtroom who has heard this portion of the testimony is ordered and instructed to keep this confidential, that is, to share it with no one, to not speak about this portion of this summary. We now move into private session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you a few questions about the 4th of August and the things that you observed in Knin on the 4th of August. At page 4 of your first statement, you describe how when the shelling began, you went to the basement of your apartment building and you stayed there with some other tenants for about half an hour and you tried to leave two or three times before you finally managed to get into your car and drive to your place of work. Now, when you said that you tried to leave the basement these two or three times, what do you mean by that? How far did you manage to get before you had to return to the basement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Well, while I was in the basement, shelling -- shells were falling and when there was a lull and a break and nothing was heard, then I tried to leave the basement but as I did so, firing would be heard again and as I didn't know what the target was, I would go back to the basement where I stayed for half an hour and only then managed to leave and get into my car and reach the station.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And of the 20 or so other people in the basement, did anyone else leave while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: No, nobody left except me because the others were mostly women and children and the building itself was a new one with new residents so all the tenants were my colleagues who were up at their positions so that the women and children didn't actually need to leave the building whereas I had my assignment of going to work, to my work post. I felt the need to be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And while you were in the basement with these women and children, what was the atmosphere? What was the emotional state of the people in the basement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Well, the emotional state was that they were frightened and filled with uncertainty and that's normal when you hear shelling all around, nobody can feel normal or not feel something. Everybody is afraid for their lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what about the other people you interacted with throughout the day in Knin? How were people reacting to the shelling? What was their emotional or psychological state at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could just get clarity in the question as to which type of people. I think in the statements we see he interacted with various categories of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please clarify, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm talking about members of the public, not people that you interacted with on any official basis, civilians in Knin that you spoke with throughout the day or interacted with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Well, that day I had a number of meetings with civilians, not many, but whoever I met, all of them were very afraid and had this presentiment of something bad happening and they were expecting this happen and thought it might -- something bad would happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: What was their reaction, if any, to the shelling that was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Well, all of them felt insecure. They felt afraid. And the essential thing was to save their lives and not come under the effects of any shelling, to remain alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in your most recent statement at paragraph 1(A), you said that at about 1300 hours on the 4th, you began to see convoys of people moving through Knin from the areas of Vrlika and Drnis. Did you start to see people leaving the town of Knin itself at some point that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: It was difficult to differentiate between people who were from Knin and others who were from Vrlika and Drnis because the roads leading from Vrlika and Drnis cross at one point, there is a crossroads and they pass through the town of Knin itself so it was difficult to say whether they belonged to a part of town, Knin town, or whether they might be from Drnis and were on their way from Drnis. So whether they belonged to Vrlika, the people coming from Vrlika or from Knin, it was difficult for me to differentiate because I didn't know the civilians much in that town.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's fine. In your statements, you describe the route that the convoy took out of Knin and out of the Krajina and you described it as being through Pasina, Otric, Srb, and Martinbrod and you also described the route as being crowded and the convoy moving very slowly. This is primarily at page 8 of your first statement. I'd like to ask you, as far as you know, was this the only route that people were taking out of the Krajina or were there others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: This route that you mentioned, the road was in the part where I spoke about Dalmatia and a part of Lika. So when speaking of Dalmatia and Lika, this is the only real road where civilians could pull out that we knew of then. In addition, I can also say that I used a mountain or actually a forest path that I hadn't known before but I was told of this path by some friends of mine but most of these civilians, they -- all of these civilians, they went towards Srb and Martinbrod taking this road.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said this was the only road where civilians could pull out. What do you mean by that? Why was that the only one that they could pull out of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Because all the other roads and crossings were checked by the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we move into private session for a moment for the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At page 8 of your first statement, you describe going from Knin to Benkovac in the early hours of the 5th of August. And in your 2007 statement at paragraph 26, you explain that you could not assess the shelling damage to the town because it was dark but you saw a few houses on fire. My question is: When you were in Benkovac, did you learn anything about whether or not anyone had been injured or killed in the shelling there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: When I arrived in Benkovac, I looked for my family members. I couldn't find them so I went to the police station where I found several men and since there was a power shortage, it was dark and they were looking for fuel for their cars and in conversation with them I heard the civilians had moved inland. No one really knew where exactly where to but they were mentioning some villages in -- near Bukovica but they couldn't tell me whether there was any casualties, any injured or killed people as a result of the shelling on the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At page 8 of your first statement you described stopping in Kistanje and Djverske on your way back to Knin from Benkovac. And you stated that everything was empty in those places and you were told by men on the street that those two places had been shelled. Can you describe what you mean by the phrase "everything was empty in those two places"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: When we stopped in Djeverske and then in Kistanje after that, I sought to find some family members but I couldn't find them or their neighbours because I wanted to ask them if they knew where they were. And as for the people that I saw on the roads in Kistanje, there was some people standing around probably waiting for some family members to join them or maybe waiting for someone to pick them up or going about their business and they told me then that these towns should be abandoned because both Kistanje and Djeverske had been shelled the previous day. They didn't tell me how severe the shelling was but there was shelling and that we should leave those places so that no one would get killed in the shelling. And then I went on on my way to Padjani.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: What was the approximate size in terms of population of those two places of Kistanje and Djeverske at that time immediately prior to the operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly what the number was. Kistanje was larger than Djeverske, it probably numbered some 1500 inhabitants. And as for Djeverske, it was to the south of Kistanje and with the hamlets around it they probably numbered around 1.000 inhabitants or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And were you aware of any military installations or equipment or anything you considered a military target in either Kistanje or Djeverske?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no military installations in Kistanje or artillery positions for long-range artillery, and the same is true of Djeverske, but not far from Djeverske, there was a facility, a brigade command, it was to the south of Djeverske, some couple of kilometres, maybe two or three to the south.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said in Kistanje, "There were no military installations in Kistanje or artillery positions for long-range artillery," was there any artillery positioning in Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in your first statement, and this is at the top of page 9, you describe the convoy as being mostly civilian but you said that there were some military personnel and vehicles in the convoy. From what you were able to observe of the convoy, were the military vehicles moving together in an organised way or were they more interspersed with the civilian vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: As far as I could observe on the road both from Knin to Benkovac and from Benkovac back, and then to Padjani and to Srb as far as I went to the convoy and drove with them, I couldn't see an organised military convoy. They were all interspersed with civilian vehicles that was used by both civilians and the military. They were all intermingled.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in your statements and in your first statement at page 9 and in paragraph 35 of your 2007 statement, you described visiting a location where the convoy had been bombed on the road from Petrovac to Bravsko on about the 7th or 8th of August and you described that you saw two trucks and several cars that had been hit. Were any of these vehicles that had been hit military vehicles, as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And where was this location exactly? Approximately how many kilometres out of Petrovac towards Bravsko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you with any precision but as far as I can recall, this was a valley where the road ran and this was about 12, 13, perhaps 15 kilometres from Petrovac to Bravsko, towards Bravsko.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Earlier in your testimony, you said that you couldn't find your family in Benkovac. Who in your family was living in Benkovac at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: At this time, my wife and her family lived in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And why were you not able to find them there on the night of the 4th and the early hours of the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Because when I arrived there, they had already left the house where they lived and gone inland and then later on to Srb and Martinbrod.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did they follow the same route that you described earlier that the convoy took, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Yes, they used the same road.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In your most recent statement at page 4, you said that at the time right before Operation Storm, there were Serb refugees living in the St. Ante monastery in Knin. How long had those refugees been living there, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: The St. Ante monastery in Knin was used by refugees in part and I don't know exactly the number of families that lived there but I knew some them because they were from my village and they had lived there since 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In your first statement at the top of page 9, you stated that, "At this time -- in the early hours of the 5th of August, almost all of the 80.000 people living in Dalmatia were trying to leave the area." I'd like to ask you what's the basis for your conclusion that almost all of the people living in Dalmatia were trying to leave the area at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Well, the main reason that they were leaving the area was that the lines of defence had been broken through, that we could not keep -- defend that area any longer so that was the reason for leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that he be allowed to finish the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, I just -- he wasn't really addressing the question that was why I stopped him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The answer is important and he should be allowed to complete it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson interrupted you when you were answering the question about the basis for your conclusion that almost all of the people living in Dalmatia were trying to leave the area at the time. You told us that the main reason was that the lines of defence had been broken through and that you could not keep, not defend that area any longer so that was the reason for leaving. Is there anything you would like to add to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to add that in my conversations both with able-bodied men and with civilians, and of course these were two different groups of men, there was a difference whether they were leaving on the 4th or on the 5th of August. So when Western Slavonia fell during Operation Flash, and when this was shown on TV Krajina and also broadcast on TV Belgrade and TV Banja Luka, many people who actually survived this, they told horror stories on how they actually had to flee the area to save their lives. So that the people in Dalmatia had this image before them, they were afraid for their lives and this is why they were leaving the area. This was the main reason why they were leaving because they could no longer feel secure there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what were the things that you saw and heard on the 4th and 5th of August that led you to conclude that almost everyone was leaving? I'm talking about your actual observations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: People were afraid for their own life and they were leaving the area. They were afraid of the shelling. And their only desire was to save their lives and the simplest way to do that was to simply move away from the front line towards Srb which was the only way out of there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson. Mr. Misetic. It will be the Gotovina Defence who will cross-examine you first. Witness 56, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Witness 56, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-056
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could now move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
